title: Uniform count-scale changes had small mean effects on a bird thermal trend in 1997-2025
abstract: We tested whether common count changes can alter a community temperature index with log(count + 1) weights. An exact derivative shows that the index can change even when all species have the same proportional count change. We audited 76,692 BBS runs on 4,785 routes in 1997-2025, with fixed thermal scores for 444 species. A gradual halving of counts changed the route fixed-effect trend by +0.000258 C per decade, against an unscaled trend of 0.04384. Simulated independent loss of detections, from full retention in 1997 to half retention in 2025, changed the mean log-weight trend by +0.000489 C per decade across 40 replicates (Monte Carlo SE 0.000046). A fixed-total log index changed the observed trend by -0.000136 C per decade. Local scale effects had opposite signs and were much larger than the pooled mean. These tests show small mean effects for the stated common-scale changes. They do not estimate historical detection loss or bound species-specific bias. Code, proofs, aggregate results and exact external input hashes are included.

display.caption: Common deterministic count changes and simulated uniform detection loss had small mean effects on CTI trends. Simulation error bars show two Monte Carlo standard errors, not uncertainty in bird population trends.
